label: Admin permissions
summary: Named permissions for a particular Django model.
why: Allows staff access to be granted per kind of record and action.
lifecycle: Django creates default model permissions after migrations; custom permissions may also be declared. Grants can change independently of the permission definition.

fields.name: id
fields.description: Stable identifier referenced by group and direct-user grants.

fields.name: name
fields.description: Readable description shown when choosing permissions.

fields.name: content_type
fields.description: Content type identifying the model this permission concerns; for example, permission to view a particular kind of record.

fields.name: codename
fields.description: Action name used in permission checks together with the application label, such as view_user.

notes: The combination of content_type and codename is unique.
Default model actions are add, change, delete, and view. These framework grants do not replace Taskiller API ownership checks.
Deleting a content type deletes its permissions; deleting a permission removes its group and direct-user grants.

label: Group permission grants
summary: Links each Django group to the permissions it grants.
why: Allows one permission to be shared by many groups and one group to grant many permissions.
lifecycle: Added or removed when a group’s permission selection changes; removed when either its group or permission is deleted.

fields.name: id
fields.description: Identifier of this individual group-to-permission grant.

fields.name: group
fields.description: Django group receiving this grant.

fields.name: permission
fields.description: Django permission granted to members of that group.

notes: Django automatically creates this through model for Group.permissions.
Each group and permission pair is unique; the row has its own stored id rather than a composite primary key.

label: Admin groups
summary: Named collections of Django permissions for staff accounts.
why: Lets administrators assign a role’s permissions once and share them across several accounts.
lifecycle: Created and renamed through Django administration or management code; membership and permission links can change. Deleting a group removes its join rows without deleting its members or permissions.

fields.name: id
fields.description: Stable identifier of this permission group.

fields.name: name
fields.description: Unique readable group name used when assigning staff roles.

notes: Group names are unique.
Groups apply to Django auth_user identities, not Taskiller users.

label: Admin group memberships
summary: Links Django accounts to the groups they belong to.
why: Lets staff inherit the permissions assigned to each of their groups.
lifecycle: Added or removed as staff group membership changes; removed when the account or group is deleted.

fields.name: id
fields.description: Identifier of this individual group membership.

fields.name: user
fields.description: Django auth_user account joining the group; not a Taskiller product account.

fields.name: group
fields.description: Django group whose permissions the account inherits.

notes: Django automatically creates this through model for User.groups.
Each user and group pair is unique. These memberships do not link to Taskiller’s users table.

label: Direct admin grants
summary: Links Django accounts directly to individual permissions.
why: Allows a staff account to receive a specific permission without changing a shared group.
lifecycle: Added or removed when direct permissions change; removed when the account or permission is deleted.

fields.name: id
fields.description: Identifier of this individual account-to-permission grant.

fields.name: user
fields.description: Django auth_user account receiving the grant; not a Taskiller product account.

fields.name: permission
fields.description: Django permission granted directly to that account.

notes: Django automatically creates this through model for User.user_permissions.
Each user and permission pair is unique. Direct grants supplement permissions inherited through groups.

label: Admin accounts
summary: Django identities used for staff sign-in and administration.
why: Gives administrators framework permissions independently of a person’s Taskiller product account.
lifecycle: Created by staff-management tools; permissions and access flags can change. Disabling an account blocks normal Django authentication; deleting it removes its group memberships, direct grants, and admin log entries.

fields.name: id
fields.description: Stable identity of this Django admin account, used by permissions and admin activity records.

fields.name: password
fields.description: Encoded password verifier used by Django authentication; never the raw password. An unusable-password marker can prevent password sign-in.

fields.name: last_login
fields.description: Last successful Django sign-in recorded for this account; empty before a login has been recorded.

fields.name: is_superuser
fields.description: Whether an active account receives all permissions without individual grants.

fields.name: username
fields.description: Unique login name for this Django account; independent of the email-based Taskiller sign-in.

fields.name: first_name
fields.description: Optional given name for the administrator; may be blank.

fields.name: last_name
fields.description: Optional family name for the administrator; may be blank.

fields.name: email
fields.description: Optional contact email for this Django identity; not the Taskiller account email and not unique by default.

fields.name: is_staff
fields.description: Whether this identity is allowed into Django administration when also active.

fields.name: is_active
fields.description: Whether normal Django authentication and permission checks treat the account as active.

fields.name: date_joined
fields.description: When this Django account was created.

notes: These are Django auth.User identities, separate from Taskiller’s users table. Creating a Taskiller account does not create an admin account.
is_staff permits entry to the admin site; model permissions still control available actions unless the active account is a superuser.
Username is unique. Email and names may be blank; blank text is different from a database NULL.

label: Model registry
summary: Identifies each Django model by its application and model name.
why: Lets permissions and admin history refer to different kinds of records through one shared model registry.
lifecycle: Populated after migrations as installed models are discovered; stale entries can be removed by Django’s content-type management command.

fields.name: id
fields.description: Stable registry identifier referenced by permissions and admin log entries.

fields.name: app_label
fields.description: Django application label containing the model.

fields.name: model
fields.description: Lowercase model name within that application.

notes: The combination of app_label and model is unique.
A content type identifies a model, not an individual record or physical table. The same model can have many records.

label: Admin browser sessions
summary: Server-side browser session records used by Django’s database session backend.
why: Keeps Django browser sign-in state on the server while the cookie carries a session key.
lifecycle: Created or updated by Django’s session backend; session keys may rotate on sign-in. Logout can remove the session, and clearsessions removes expired records.

fields.name: session_key
fields.description: Random browser-session lookup key, also used in the session cookie; identifies this record.

fields.name: session_data
fields.description: Encoded and signed session contents, which may include the Django account identity and authentication state; not a raw password.

fields.name: expire_date
fields.description: When this server-side browser session expires and becomes eligible for cleanup.

notes: These support Django browser sessions, including admin cookies. They are separate from Taskiller’s API auth_sessions and refresh_tokens.
The stored session payload is signed and encoded, not encrypted; it must not be presented as raw public guide data.
There is no user foreign key: authentication state, when present, is inside the encoded session payload.
expire_date is indexed for expiry cleanup. Messages uses no dedicated model table.

label: Admin activity
summary: Records additions, changes, and deletions made through Django administration.
why: Shows administrators who performed an admin action and which record it concerned.
lifecycle: Written by Django admin actions; object deletion can leave its historical representation in the log. Deleting the acting Django account removes its log entries; deleting a content type clears that link.

fields.name: id
fields.description: Identifier of this individual admin activity record.

fields.name: action_time
fields.description: When the admin action was recorded.

fields.name: user
fields.description: Django account that performed the admin action.

fields.name: content_type
fields.description: Model of the affected object; may be empty if its content type has been removed or was unavailable.

fields.name: object_id
fields.description: Identifier of the affected object, kept as text so different model key formats fit; may be empty when no identifier was supplied.

fields.name: object_repr
fields.description: Readable description of the object captured for history, even if the object is later deleted.

fields.name: action_flag
fields.description: Whether the action added (1), changed (2), or deleted (3) the object.

fields.name: change_message
fields.description: Details of the edit for admin history; may be structured JSON text or a plain explanation, and may be blank.

notes: The user relation points to Django auth_user, not Taskiller’s users table.
content_type plus object_id describes the affected object; object_id is text, not a foreign key to that object’s table.
This table is not protected by Taskiller’s immutable session-event or security-event triggers.
change_message can hold structured JSON describing edits or a plain message; its storage is text.

label: Migration history
summary: Records which Django schema migrations have been applied.
why: Lets Django determine which schema changes still need to run and which changes can be reversed.
lifecycle: The migration recorder creates its table when needed, records successful application, and removes records on reversal. Fake migration operations can change this history without executing the corresponding schema changes.

fields.name: id
fields.description: Identifier of this migration-history entry.

fields.name: app
fields.description: Application label whose migration was recorded.

fields.name: name
fields.description: Migration name within the application, such as the initial migration name.

fields.name: applied
fields.description: When Django recorded the migration as applied.

notes: This is MigrationRecorder.Migration, included explicitly because it is not a normal installed application model.
Rows record migration state, not the migration code, schema contents, or a database backup.
